Like if he met those eyes for real, something might fracture beyond repair. The silence wasn’t just awkward. It was dense. Suspended. Like the Fog itself was watching, waiting to see who would break first. No one spoke. Even Jill — who could usually be counted on to cut tension with a well-placed snort or tactical sarcasm — had gone still. Her earlier irritation had banked into silence, burning low like the coals. But her eyes kept straying to Felix. Not worried. Not exactly. Just... tracking. He only looked calm to someone that wasn’t familiar with quite rage, and she was waiting to see if the fault line in him would hold. The longer the silence went on for, the heavier it felt. It settled between them — dense, restless. Lacking in the peace that should have come with healing wounds and building fatigue. Thick enough that it felt like a fifth presence in the circle, sitting between them with smoke on its breath. Unable to stand the tension, David shifted. He set the mug down beside him with a soft ceramic clink, fingers lingering around it like maybe, if he was lucky, it would swallow him whole. He stared at the fire. Then the cup. Then the dirt. Finally, cautiously, like he had to test the air first — he cleared his throat. “...You gonna yell at me again?” Felix didn’t look over. Didn’t blink. “No,” he said softly, firelight catching on the leftover dust that still coated his hair. “I got it out of my system.” A pause. “...You sure?” “No.” David tried to take a deeper breath to steady himself — he regretted it immediately. His ribs flared under the bruises, a deep ache that echoed through his torso. He winced lightly against the sensation, shifting his pose the smallest amount to take the excess pressure off. The next trial was going to suck if he couldn’t even take a deep breath without folding in half. That was, assuming Felix didn’t just cripple him before the night was done. Not that he wouldn’t have deserved it. Felix glanced over, the motion subtle but sharp. His expression was unreadable, carved into something just shy of composed. A careful arrangement of clear restraint — like someone trying very hard not to say something they’d regret. “I’m not mad you got hurt,” His voice didn’t rise. Didn’t waver. “I’m mad you hid it. From me. ” That landed. Not just as a reprimand — there was a strong tone of betrayal under it. David’s gaze dropped instantly, back to the fire, like maybe if he stared hard enough the flames would explain what the hell he was supposed to say. “...Didn’t think it mattered,” he muttered, after too long. Felix’s jaw flexed — just once. Quiet. Controlled. Just enough to say: wrong answer. “I didn’t want you two to panic,” David said, softer now. His voice scraped low, like it was trying not to shake. “Didn’t think it’d help if I made it a thing. Figured... if I kept quiet, we’d all get through it faster. You guys didn’t need the extra stress in the moment.” He hesitated, then added — too quiet: “Didn’t think anyone would notice if I just didn’t say anything.” He had meant it as a shield. A half-hearted excuse, a clumsy patch on the crawlspace he’d built to hide the worst of it. It landed more like a door slamming shut. Felix turned his head — slow, sharp, deliberate. “Do you think I wouldn’t have eventually noticed?” he asked, the firelight caught in his eyes, gleaming through the crack in his voice. “You seriously think I wouldn’t care?” David flinched internally. Not from pain — that, at least, had dulled to a manageable throb under the Fog’s numb haze. But that ? That low, even voice from Felix — no raised tone, no sarcasm, just open truth dropped on him like a stone. That hurt something deep in his chest that flared worse than the damage to his ribs had. “It’s not that,” David said quickly, too quickly. The words spilled like he was trying to plug the hole with excuses. Felix didn’t interrupt. Didn’t argue. Didn’t save him from the silence that followed. Somehow, that was worse. David raked a hand back through his hair, fingers catching in dried blood along the way and twitching lightly against the pull, like the sting was deserved. “I’ve always handled my shit,” he muttered. “That’s what I do. ” His voice hardened, not in anger, but defense. Old habits surfacing like bruises under skin. “People don’t need to babysit me. They need me solid. If I fall apart — what the fuck happens to the rest of you?” It was a deflection. A wall built out of duty. It sounded flimsy even as he had said it. “And what happens if you die?” Quiet. Even. “You think that won’t break something?” David didn’t answer. He couldn’t. Because suddenly, he wasn’t sure. The silence stretched again — not empty this time, but taut. Like a wire pulled too tight between two bodies while everyone else was pretending they couldn’t hear it hum. Jill nudged a stick in the fire with the toe of her boot. She watched the sparks jump like it was the most fascinating thing she’d seen all day. Anything to keep her eyes off them . Dwight, on the other side of the circle, was rewrapping the same strip of cloth around his arm for the third time. Not because it needed fixing. Because it gave his hands something to do.
